subject: botany
question_text: Who proposed five kingdom classification? How many kingdoms of this classification contain eukaryotes?

verification.note: Sourced from the Junior Fastrack botany book, Biological Classification chapter (book pp.4-5), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star ranks and NO year citations. Only ONE source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely pending: 'not checked' must never be read as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Proposer
steps.why: Naming the scientist with the year and listing the five kingdoms sets up the count the second part of the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Writing Linnaeus. Linnaeus gave the two kingdom system; Whittaker gave five.
Missing one kingdom from the list — usually Protista.
steps.memory_tip: Whittaker, 1969, five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
steps.margin_note: Name plus year is the safe form; the list supports the second part.

steps.label: Eukaryotic kingdoms

lines.text: Four kingdoms of the five contain eukaryotes.

steps.why: Only bacteria and cyanobacteria (kingdom Monera) are prokaryotic, so the remaining four kingdoms are all eukaryotic.
common_mistakes: Answering five. Monera is prokaryotic, so the eukaryotic count is four.
Placing Protista with the prokaryotes. Protists are eukaryotic.
steps.memory_tip: Five kingdoms minus Monera = four eukaryotic kingdoms.
steps.margin_note: The number four with the four names is the full second mark.

insider_note: The second part is the catch: many students write five; subtracting Monera gives the marked answer, four.
